source: Wikipedia: Expected value of sample information
finding: EVSI is the expected gain in utility from seeing a sample before deciding. It is computed before any data is seen (preposterior analysis). EVSI = E[U|SI] minus E[U], where E[U|SI] averages the best posterior-optimal utility over all possible samples z.
numbers: Formula: EVSI = integral of max_d E[U(d,x)|z] p(z) dz minus max_d E[U(d,x)]. Worked example: a Dirichlet prior over 5 outcome proportions, a multinomial trial of n=100, approve only if posterior mean utility > 0. No EVSI numbers given (graph only).
quote: the expected increase in utility that a decision-maker could obtain
limits: Secondary source, tagged as needing citations. It credits Schlaifer and Raiffa with popularising the idea in the 1960s and cites the 1968 MIT Press printing.
agent_relevance: The agent can treat a noisy test as a lottery over posteriors. The test is worth running only if some possible result would flip the action.

source: Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961) Applied Statistical Decision Theory (Harvard Business School)
finding: Founding text. It introduced preposterior analysis and EVSI as a decision tool, and gave conjugate-prior closed forms. Seen here only through later papers; the book itself was not available to open.
numbers: Per Fleischhacker et al.: closed-form EVSI under quadratic loss for a Bernoulli process with Beta prior is in Table 6.2, p.191. Three desiderata for a value-of-information formula (tractable, rich, interpretable) are on p.44.
limits: Not opened. Page numbers come from a 2023 citing paper (edition may differ). A web search snippet also credits Schlaifer (1959) with the first EVSI statement.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact vocabulary for our noisy-test step: prior, likelihood of result, posterior, best action after each result, average over results.

source: Chavez and Henrion (1994) Efficient Estimation of the Value of Information in Monte Carlo Models
finding: Defines EVPI and EVI by preposterior analysis for Monte Carlo decision models. Key trick: let z be the value gap between the best and second-best decision. Assume it is linear in the inputs, fit by regression on the samples, and integrate the negative tail. EVPI is the integral of |z| over z<0 weighted by its density.
numbers: Applied to a military evacuation planning model: 27 courses of action, over 100 inputs, 9 probabilistic. Perfect-information value of citizens in the capital about 6 lives; transfer rate in the capital more than 7 lives. Nine perfect-information values took 1 min 53 s on a Macintosh IIfx.
limits: Linear value assumption and a normal assumption for z. Only two decisions compared at once. Authors list accuracy versus an exact method as future work (not tested).
agent_relevance: Shows the cheap way to rank which uncertainty is worth testing: value of information is low when no plausible result changes the best action.

source: Chavez and Henrion (1994), same paper: Relative Information Multiple
finding: Partial information is expressed as a Relative Information Multiple (RIM): prior variance divided by posterior variance on a variable. A test with RIM k leaves a fraction 1/k of the variance. This puts a noisy test on a scale between no information (k=1) and perfect information (k to infinity).
numbers: RIM k = prior variance / posterior variance. The preposterior variance of z is built from these multiples (exact factor garbled in the text extraction, not recorded). EVI = integral over the negative part of the preposterior density of z.
limits: Normal approximation; a heuristic proposal, not tested against ground truth.
agent_relevance: A direct way to turn test quality (how much it narrows belief) into a number the program can compute, rather than the model guessing 'this test is useful'.

source: Heath, Manolopoulou and Baio (2017) Efficient Monte Carlo Estimation of EVSI using Moment Matching
finding: Estimates EVSI by matching moments of the preposterior mean of the net benefit instead of nesting simulations. The variance of the preposterior mean equals prior variance minus expected posterior variance.
numbers: Test model (Ades et al.): 4 uncertain inputs of 11. Four studies: 60 patients (side effects), 100 patients (quality of life), RCT 200 per arm (odds ratio), same RCT on two inputs. 1,330,000 simulations total. Posterior variance step 3.8 to 6.1 s. Comparators: Strong et al. regression 8.4 s; nested Monte Carlo 207,595 s (about 2.4 days).
limits: Bias is upward and large for small future samples; accurate when future sample size is above about 20. Needs the posterior variance to be estimable.
agent_relevance: Shows EVSI can be found without full nested simulation. For the agent: approximate with a variance reduction proxy when a test is cheap to model.

source: Heath and Baio (2017) Calculating EVSI using Efficient Nested Monte Carlo: A Tutorial
finding: Tutorial for the efficient nested method. Compute effort should go to the number of outer data simulations, not the number of inner posterior draws. Moment matching should only be used with more than 30 outer samples.
numbers: Two inner sizes: 500,000 (108 to 129 s per estimate) and 5,000 (9 to 17 s). Outer values 20 to 100, 200 repeats each. Gold-standard bias check used 100,000 x 100,000 at about 60 days. Rule: total simulations divided by posterior draws gives the outer count (50,000 / 1,000 = 50).
limits: Slight upward bias, large at 20 outer samples.
agent_relevance: Cost of valuing a test can exceed the cost of running it. The scaffold should use a crude closed-form or coarse estimate, not a deep one.

source: Heath, Kunst et al. (2019) Calculating EVSI in Practice: Considerations from Three Case Studies
finding: A consortium compared four EVSI approximation methods on three published health models, including multiple outcomes, missing data and an observational study. The approximate methods agreed enough to be usable.
numbers: Approximate methods took minutes or hours for reasonably accurate EVSI. Traditional nested Monte Carlo took weeks. In one example, using all 100,000 simulations took more than 2 hours for a method.
limits: Three models only, all health economics. Methods differ in what skills they need.
agent_relevance: Independent cross-check that fast EVSI approximations are close to the slow gold standard.

source: Kunst et al. (2019) Computing EVSI Efficiently: Expertise and Skills Required for Four Model-Based Methods
finding: Compares four approximation methods by inputs and skills. All four need probabilistic sensitivity analysis output. One needs the model re-run for each EVSI estimate. Users need regression, likelihood specification or Bayesian skills.
numbers: Four methods; software is in R; two have online apps. No timing table beyond the companion paper.
limits: A practical guide, not an accuracy test.
agent_relevance: Setup cost matters: a method that needs a model re-run for every test is too costly in a thinking loop.

source: Hironaka, Giles, Goda and Thom (2020) Multilevel Monte Carlo estimation of EVSI
finding: Nested Monte Carlo for EVSI costs O(eps^(-2-1/alpha)) for accuracy eps, where alpha (between 1/2 and 1) is the bias rate. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces this to the optimal O(eps^-2).
numbers: Cost exponent: nested -2-1/alpha, so at alpha=1/2 cost goes as eps^-4; multilevel eps^-2. Numerical experiments confirm large savings (figures not quoted here).
limits: Assumptions on decision and information models; finite set of decisions.
agent_relevance: EVSI is a nested expectation: an outer average over test results of an inner best-action choice. Cost grows fast with precision.

source: Heath (2021) Calculating EVSI Adjusting for Imperfect Implementation
finding: Classic EVSI assumes the better treatment is adopted fully and at once after the study. Two new methods let adoption depend on the strength of evidence.
numbers: Maximum difference between the two methods at most 6% in all three examples. The efficient method was 6 to 60 times faster than nested simulation.
limits: Three health examples. Implementation model is assumed.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: information has value only if the agent acts on it. If the scaffold ignores or half-applies a test result, EVSI overstates the gain.

source: Fleischhacker, Fok, Madiman and Wu (2023) A Closed-Form EVSI Expression for a Multinomial Data-Generating Process
finding: Generalises the Raiffa-Schlaifer beta-Binomial EVSI to integer data with a Dirichlet prior. Gives closed forms for EVSI, expected value of distribution information, and the best sample size.
numbers: Optimal sample size has three terms: prior strength, ratio of quadratic-loss scale to unit sampling cost, and data variance. Zero sample if the fixed cost K cannot be recovered. Quotes Lindley that sample size is 'embarrassingly difficult to answer'.
limits: Quadratic loss; conjugate priors only. The paper notes value of information need not be monotone in action flexibility, risk aversion or wealth.
agent_relevance: Closed forms exist for the simplest test-quality cases, so the program can compute them exactly instead of asking the model.

source: Fleischhacker et al. (2023), same paper: table of conjugate EVSI cases
finding: Lists data-generating processes that already had closed-form EVSI: Bernoulli with Beta, Poisson with Gamma, Normal with known or unknown variance, Multinomial with Dirichlet. Most source formulas trace to Raiffa and Schlaifer.
numbers: Table lists each process with its conjugate prior and a source; the Bernoulli, Normal and Multinomial rows cite the 1961 book.
limits: Reading of a table; row-by-row detail not checked against the book.
agent_relevance: A short list of cases the agent can compute exactly when a test is a repeated yes/no check.

source: Sadatsafavi et al. (2024) EVSI for external validation of risk prediction models
finding: Applies EVSI to deciding how big a validation study should be. EVSI rises with sample size and levels off at EVPI. The value can be zero when current evidence already settles the decision.
numbers: Case study: 500 current patients, 43 events; Beta(44, 458) for prevalence. EVPI at threshold 0.01 was 0.00037, at 0.02 was 0.00125, and 0 at 0.05 and 0.10 (so EVSI 0 for any N). At 0.02, N = 1,000 gave EVSI 0.00101 (about 81% of EVPI); little gain beyond N = 4,000.
limits: One cardiac case study. Scaled to 800,000 US cases a year: 806 true positives gained or 39,500 false positives avoided per year at N=1,000.
agent_relevance: Diminishing returns and a hard zero are both visible: a noisy test is worthless when the decision is far from the threshold. This supports a rule to skip tests when the answer is already clear.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Agent simulates future answers to a candidate question, scores each question by expected information gain, propagates reward through a tree and asks the best one. This is a one-step EVSI-like choice with entropy gain as the value.
numbers: Average success rate +38.1% over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; +46.6% for Llama3-70B. Troubleshooting with GPT-4: 43.7% to 67.3%. Medical DX GPT-4: 97.0%. MedDG: 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro), 88.0% (GPT-4). Beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, adapted ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Simplified yes/no benchmarks; GPT-4 plays the answerer. Authors note answers may not fully eliminate options. Simulation limited to 3 steps for budget.
agent_relevance: Evidence that choosing the question by computed expected information gain beats free-form asking. The program can do the scoring.

source: Hu et al. (2024), same paper: equal-compute and reward ablations
finding: Gain does not come from more tokens alone. At matched GPT-4 token use, pruned UoT still beats ToT and CoT-SC. Swapping ToT's self-evaluation reward for the information-gain reward adds accuracy.
numbers: Information-gain reward in ToT adds about 5.9% on average. Adapted-ToT raised to depth 4 (matched cost) still below UoT depth 3. Table 2: CoT-SC (k=33) at 4.6k tokens scored 32.6 (20Q), 37.6 (MD), 42.5 (TB). A t-test shows significance (Appendix H).
limits: GPT-4 used throughout the ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrail G7 (pay for itself at equal tokens) and G5 (code computes scores, not model self-ratings).

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni and Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Llama 2-Chat 7B samples many questions per 20-Questions game; pairs of high-EIG and low-EIG questions train DPO. Questions get more informative and games shorter. Plain supervised fine-tuning lowers success.
numbers: Candidate set of 8, DPO vs zero-shot: INLG 68.9% vs 56.7% success (S@1), 5.2 vs 7.1 questions, EIG 0.45 vs 0.34. Things 61.1% vs 51.1%, 5.2 vs 7.5, EIG 0.40 vs 0.29. Celebrities 72.2% vs 71.1%, 5.1 vs 7.6, EIG 0.47 vs 0.35. Fine-tuning only (FT): 46.6%, 42.2%, 46.7%.
limits: Small 7B model; yes/no 20 Questions only. In a second table the hypothesis-scanning versus constraint-seeking mix shifts. Celebrities gain in S@1 is marginal.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot LLM questions are far from the information-optimal ones; the gap can be closed, but needs training or external scoring.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov and Ellis (2024) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLM proposes 8 candidate questions; a probabilistic model whose conditionals come from prompting scores each by expected entropy reduction (equal to expected model change); the best is asked. Beats vanilla and ReAct prompting.
numbers: 150 simplified web-shopping tasks of 10 products from WebShop. GPT-4 for every method, simulated user by GPT-4. Entropy-reduction LLM beat both baselines from the second question; three questions of it beat four of the baselines. Exact scores were in figures only.
limits: Yes/no questions only; simulated users; product set of 10. At the fourth question the vanilla LLM gained more information, but little was left.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as UoT: propose with the model, score by computed information gain in code, ask the top one.

source: Handa et al. (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN uses Bayesian optimal experimental design to choose the pairwise question and an LM to name features and phrase the question. It beats pure LM and pure BOED questioning in a human study, measured by time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA).
numbers: Metric TIDA is the area under accuracy-gain over turns. Results shown as bars with one standard error; text states OPEN beats LM pairwise questions and BOED without verbalisation. Open-ended LM questions scored higher under LM prediction but lost the OPEN prediction advantage.
limits: Exact score values not in text (figure only). Small user study; user fatigue and repeated questions seen in some chats.
agent_relevance: Hybrid division of labour that matches our schema: LM makes language, program does the information math.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu and van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design over the LLM's own sampled solutions. Questions chosen by expected information gain (EIG) beat those found by asking the LLM to reason about questions.
numbers: Coding with 4 added requirements, 48 non-trivial tasks (APPS and HumanEval, zero-shot 35% and 70% for GPT-4o-mini), 3 runs and 3 evaluation seeds, 4 models. EIG strategies gave higher accuracy with fewer test cases queried; open-answer questions beat binary ones. Gap shrinks for stronger models.
limits: Needs many extra LLM calls. Task filtering to non-trivial tasks. Exact accuracy values in figures and appendix tables.
agent_relevance: Gain shrinks as the model grows; the value of a question is lower when the prior is already strong. Worth testing at equal tokens (G7).

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman and Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Language models ask users open questions or edge cases to learn intent. In pre-registered studies this often beats user-written prompts or labelled examples.
numbers: 388 participants over 3 domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning). GATE beat user-written prompts in 6 of 10 settings (absolute) and 7 of 10 (area under curve). Generative yes/no questions beat prompts in every setting. Significant against no elicitation in all but email.
limits: Significance against baselines only in content recommendation and email. Low power in moral reasoning. Informativeness not computed as EIG.
agent_relevance: Asking has measurable value but varies by domain, and some domains show no significant gain.

source: Ren et al. (2023) Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for LLM Planners (KnowNo)
finding: Uses conformal prediction on LLM option probabilities so the robot asks for help only when its prediction set has more than one option, with a coverage guarantee. This trades help cost against success.
numbers: Hardware tabletop (50 trials): KnowNo (1-eps = 0.75): plan success 0.76, task success 0.74, set size 1.72, help 0.58 per step and 0.92 per trial; Simple Set (1-eps = 0.58, matched plan success 0.76): task success 0.72, set size 2.04, help 0.72 and 1.00. No-help baseline: plan 0.41, task 0.38. Help cut by 14% step-wise, 8% trial-wise; 10 to 24% in simulation.
limits: Needs a calibration set. Option probabilities from the LLM may be miscalibrated. Small number of hardware trials.
agent_relevance: A guaranteed way to decide when to ask. The asking threshold comes from calibration data, not from the model's own wording.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update beliefs well when evidence arrives over several rounds. They plateau after the first interaction, unlike an exact Bayesian assistant. Fine-tuning on Bayesian assistant traces narrows the gap and transfers to other tasks.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds. Bayesian Assistant final accuracy 81%; random 37%; off-the-shelf models mostly in the 36 to 58% range; humans (48 users) below the Bayesian assistant. Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time.
limits: Chain-of-thought, 30 rounds, numerical formats and base models did not fix updating. Tuned on one task, tested on related ones.
agent_relevance: A noisy test is only useful if the agent updates correctly on it. LLMs do this poorly, so the program should do the update (G5).

source: Suri et al. (2026) Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents (SAGE-Agent)
finding: Uses expected value of perfect information over tool-parameter domains to pick which clarifying question to ask, with a cost term for redundant questions. Used for inference-time selection and as an RL reward.
numbers: Ambiguous tasks: coverage 59.73% vs 55.70% (domain-aware ReAct), 54.12% (ProCOT), 52.34% (ReAct); 1.39 questions per ambiguous task, 45.7% fewer than domain-aware ReAct and 59.4% fewer than active task disambiguation. When2Call accuracy 36.5% to 65.2% (3B) and 36.7% to 62.9% (7B) after uncertainty-weighted GRPO. Raising the question penalty from 0 to 0.5 cut questions 18.1% with under 3% change in coverage.
limits: Tool-calling benchmark with simulated user answers; EVPI here is an upper bound used as a proxy for the value of a question.
agent_relevance: A recent direct use of value of information for an agent, including the stopping rule: ask only if expected gain exceeds question cost.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024), same paper: equivalence of two question scores
finding: Shows that choosing the question with least expected posterior entropy is the same as choosing the one with greatest expected model change, because the expected cross-entropy term is identical for all questions.
numbers: Appendix A.1 proof; 8 questions sampled from the proposal per turn; sampling one question reduces the method to the vanilla LLM.
limits: Holds for the paper's discrete hypothesis model with yes/no answers.
agent_relevance: Gives one simple score for ranking questions (information gain) that code can compute from a table of hypotheses and answer likelihoods.

source: Qiu et al. (2026), same paper: failed fixes for weak belief updating
finding: Several simple remedies did not help LLMs update on evidence: chain-of-thought prompts, a purely numeric option format, 30 instead of 5 rounds, and base models. Only training on Bayesian-assistant traces helped.
numbers: Oracle teaching (always-correct assistant) helped but Bayesian teaching helped more; Bayesian-tuned models matched the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time.
limits: Open-weight 7B to 70B models plus GPT-4.1 and Gemini 1.5 in the baseline; fine-tuning only on open models.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on prompts to make the model treat a noisy test result with the right weight. Keep the posterior update in code.
